title: Sheaf Cohomology Background
notes: Use the opening to establish the contract for the appendix. The notebook already asks students to identify an object, an allowed perturbation, and an invariant; here those words become sheaves, restrictions, stalks, and cohomology groups. Emphasize that the source span is not a detour from complex geometry but the language that later lets local analytic constructions be compared globally.

title: Presheaves Are Restriction Machines
notes: Introduce a presheaf as a disciplined bookkeeping device. The open sets become a category by inclusion, while the assigned groups or rings move contravariantly through restriction maps. The identity and composition rules mean that restricting in one step or several steps gives the same answer. This is still only bookkeeping; no gluing has been promised yet.

title: The Two Sheaf Axioms
notes: The key distinction from a presheaf is that local data can be trusted. Separatedness says local tests detect equality, while gluing says compatible local pieces assemble into a unique global piece. Use continuous functions as the sanity check: if the functions agree on overlaps, the pasted function is well defined, and continuity remains local.

title: Examples: Functions, Constants, Sections
notes: This comparison is where students often repair their intuition. A constant presheaf remembers one number per open set, so it cannot glue different constants across disconnected components. The constant sheaf instead means locally constant functions. Then move to vector bundles: the sheaf of sections is not extra decoration, because for many purposes the bundle can be recovered from its section sheaf.

title: Homomorphisms and the Image-Cokernel Trap
notes: The commutative square gives a clean test for a sheaf homomorphism: map first and restrict later, or restrict first and map later, and the result must match. Then stress the asymmetric behavior. Kernels are local equalizers and stay sheaves. Images and cokernels can fail gluing, so the source defines image and cokernel sheaves by sheafifying the naive presheaves.

title: Stalks: Germs Seen Under a Microscope
notes: A stalk is the formal version of looking only near one point. The representative section and the representative neighborhood may change, as long as the two representatives coincide after passing to a smaller neighborhood of the point. This is why stalks detect sheaf exactness and surjectivity: every question has been reduced to a sufficiently small local lifting problem.

title: Sheafification Repairs a Presheaf
notes: Sheafification is best presented as the universal repair operation. It does not invent arbitrary functions into stalks; every germ-valued section has to be locally represented by a genuine section of the original presheaf. If the presheaf was already a sheaf, this construction changes nothing. Otherwise it adds precisely the missing gluing behavior.

title: Exactness Is Stalkwise, But Global Sections Are Fragile
notes: Exactness for sheaves is local in the strongest possible way: after passing to stalks, exactness can be checked point by point. The surprise is that taking global sections does not preserve the right end of a short exact sequence. Cohomology is introduced precisely to measure this failure of global lifting, not as an arbitrary new invariant.

title: Flasque Resolutions Supply Cohomology-Free Objects
notes: This slide corrects the common OCR noise in the source span: the intended term is flasque. The intuition is that a section over a smaller open set can be extended all the way to the whole space. The source uses flasque sheaves as the chosen acyclic class, then states that every sheaf admits a flasque resolution, so the definition applies generally.

title: Defining H^i(M,F)
notes: The definition is deliberately procedural. Replace the sheaf by a flasque resolution, apply global sections to get an honest complex of groups or vector spaces, and take ordinary cohomology. Point out the two calibration facts: degree zero recovers global sections, and a flasque sheaf has no higher cohomology. Independence of the chosen resolution is what makes the procedure an invariant.

title: Short Exact Sequences Produce Long Exact Sequences
notes: Present the long exact sequence as the central payoff. A short exact sequence of sheaves may lose surjectivity on global sections, but the connecting homomorphism records exactly where the obstruction lives. For later complex geometry, this is the computational mechanism behind many extension, deformation, and classification arguments.

title: Euler-Poincare Characteristic
notes: Euler-Poincare characteristic is a compressed numerical shadow of all cohomology groups. The alternating signs are not decoration; in a long exact sequence, dimensions cancel in adjacent degrees, which gives additivity for short exact sequences. This makes the invariant useful even when individual cohomology groups are hard to compute.

title: Soft and Acyclic Sheaves
notes: After the abstract flasque construction, the appendix points to more usable acyclic sheaves. Softness is phrased with closed subsets rather than open subsets, and on manifolds it aligns with extension tools such as partitions of unity. The warning about holomorphic functions is important for complex geometry: analytic rigidity prevents the same soft argument from applying.

title: Cech Cohomology From a Cover
notes: Cech cohomology is the cover-based version of the same local-to-global idea. A zero-cochain gives local sections, a one-cochain gives overlap data, and higher cochains live on higher intersections. The alternating differential is the algebraic way of saying that overlap corrections must be compatible. Refinement is how the construction avoids depending on one particular cover.

title: Basic Cech Computations
notes: Use the circle computation as a model of how a cover remembers topology. The two open arcs are individually simple, but their intersection has two pieces, and that split creates the one-dimensional cohomology class. Then connect this to the broader statements in the source: spheres and projective spaces follow similar patterns, and degree-one Cech cohomology is especially reliable.

title: Line Bundles, Pullbacks, Stalks, and Fibres
notes: Close by combining the two final uses of the appendix. Degree-one Cech cohomology classifies line bundles by transition functions, while inverse image and ringed-space pullback explain how sheaves move along maps. End with the stalk-versus-fibre distinction: a stalk stores all local germs near the point, while the fibre is a quotient and matches the geometric fibre for vector bundles.
